etymology: Hebrew maskīl, from sākal, “to be wise, to instruct, to deal prudently”; a psalm of instruction or contemplation — a teaching-song that makes the singer wise.
biblical_def: Maschil is the title borne by thirteen psalms (32, 42, 44, 45, 52–55, 74, 78, 88, 89, 142), drawn from the Hebrew root that signifies wisdom and instruction. It marks a psalm not merely felt but understood — a didactic song that teaches the people of God the ways of God. The same root sounds in the charge, “sing ye praises with understanding” (Psa 47:7), for the worship of the LORD is never a mindless rapture but a reasonable service. The chief example is the thirty-second psalm, David’s great Maschil of forgiveness, opening “Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven” and proceeding to teach: “I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go” (Psa 32:8). So the Maschil weds doctrine to praise; it informs the mind while it warms the heart. The apostle keeps the same order under the new covenant, bidding the church let the word of Christ dwell in her richly, “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms” (Col 3:16). Let the believer learn that true worship instructs; the song that leaves the worshipper no wiser in the things of God, however it stirs him, is no Maschil. The affections must be fed through the understanding, that the whole man may bless the LORD.
webster_summary: A psalm of instruction or contemplation; a teaching-song that weds sound doctrine to holy praise.
webster_full: MASCHIL, a Hebrew term in the titles of thirteen psalms, signifying a psalm of instruction, understanding, or contemplation.
It is derived from a root meaning to be wise, to instruct, or to act prudently.
It marks a psalm meant to teach the people of God, that the affections may be moved through an informed mind.
The same root underlies the charge to sing praises with understanding.
It witnesses that the worship of the LORD is a reasonable service, never a mindless rapture.
scriptures: I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go: I will guide thee with mine eye.
For God is the King of all the earth: sing ye praises with understanding.
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
corruption_summary: The Maschil rebukes the modern divorce of worship from instruction, where praise is measured by feeling rather than by the truth it teaches.
corruption_paragraphs: The age prizes a worship of pure sensation — the swelling sound, the heightened mood, the experience that leaves nothing behind but the memory of having felt much. Against this the Maschil sets its very name: a song that instructs, that sends the worshipper away wiser in the ways of God. Where the affections are stirred but the understanding is left empty, the worshipper has had a feeling, not a Maschil.

The principle to recover is that the heart is reached through the head, not around it. David’s teaching-psalms move the soul precisely by teaching it — of pardon, of providence, of the judgments of God. Reformed worship has always been word-filled for this reason: the song that carries the most doctrine, sung with grace, warms the affections most truly and most lastingly.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for wisdom and instruction, Maschil names a psalm that teaches the worshipper even as it moves him to praise.
roots_lines: Maschil — Hebrew maskīl, from sākal, to be wise or to instruct.
It heads thirteen psalms, among them the great penitential Maschil of Psalm 32.
The same root sounds in “sing ye praises with understanding” (Psa 47:7).
It marks a song that informs the mind while it warms the heart.
The apostle keeps its order: teaching and admonishing one another in psalms (Col 3:16).
usage: A true Maschil sends the worshipper away wiser in the things of God, not merely moved.
Like David’s teaching-psalms, sound worship reaches the affections through an instructed mind.
Sing ye praises with understanding: the song that teaches no truth, however stirring, is no Maschil.

etymology: Hebrew miktām, of uncertain root; by the ancient reckoning from ketem, “fine gold” (a golden or precious psalm), or from kātam, “to engrave, to inscribe” (a graven memorial); borne by six psalms.
biblical_def: Michtam titles six psalms of David — the sixteenth and the fifty-sixth through the sixtieth — five of them prayers wrung from the midst of mortal danger. The word is read by the godly two ways, and both are precious. If it signifies “a golden psalm,” it marks these as jewels to be treasured; if “an inscription” or “graven thing,” it makes them memorials engraved for lasting witness, as a man cuts in stone what he would not have forgotten. The sixteenth psalm is the Michtam of the resurrection: “thou wilt not leave my soul in hell; neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption” (Psa 16:10). Both Peter and Paul preach this very verse as the prophecy of Christ’s rising, for David, being dead, saw corruption, but the Holy One did not (Act 2:27; 13:35). Here then is gold indeed, and an inscription that outlasts every monument of men: the promise of an undecaying Saviour, graven into the Psalter a thousand years before the empty tomb. Let the saint treasure these golden psalms, hiding them in the heart against the day of trouble, when David’s God will prove again a refuge to all who trust in Him.
webster_summary: A golden or graven psalm; a precious memorial-song of David, the chief being the Michtam of the resurrection.
webster_full: MICHTAM, a Hebrew word in the titles of six psalms of David, of uncertain but rich derivation.
It is referred by some to a root signifying fine gold, and by others to a root signifying to engrave or inscribe.
Thus it marks a psalm either as a golden treasure or as a graven memorial set up for lasting witness.
Five of the six are prayers offered from the midst of danger and deliverance.
The chief is the sixteenth psalm, the Michtam of the resurrection of Christ.
scriptures: For thou wilt not leave my soul in hell; neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption.
Because thou wilt not leave my soul in hell, neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption.
To the chief Musician upon Jonathelemrechokim, Michtam of David, when the Philistines took him in Gath.
corruption_summary: These are messianic gold; the entry faces no postmodern redefinition, but the modern reluctance to read the Psalter as prophecy of Christ would melt the gold down to mere ancient verse.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet there is a live error to name: the modern habit of reading the Psalms as nothing more than the religious poetry of an ancient people, with the messianic promises explained away as later idealism rather than true prediction. By that reckoning the sixteenth psalm is only David hoping not to die young, and its gold is melted down to common metal.

The principle to recover is the apostolic reading of the Psalter. Peter and Paul did not allegorize Psalm 16; they preached it as plain prophecy, observing that David died and saw corruption, so that the undecaying Holy One must be Another — the risen Christ (Act 2:29–31). The Michtam is gold precisely because Christ is its substance; the saint who treasures it is treasuring Him.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for fine gold or for an engraving, Michtam names a precious, memorial psalm of David crowned by the prophecy of the resurrection.

usage: The Michtam of the resurrection is gold indeed: the promise of an undecaying Saviour graven into the Psalter.
Treasure these golden psalms in the heart against the day of trouble.
Peter preached Psalm 16 as plain prophecy, not poetry: David saw corruption, but the Holy One did not.

etymology: Hebrew shiggāyōn, perhaps from shāgāh, “to reel, to wander, to go astray”; a wild and irregular ode, a song of strong and varied emotion; the plural shigiōnōth heads the prayer of Habakkuk.
biblical_def: Shiggaion titles the seventh psalm, “which David sang unto the LORD, concerning the words of Cush the Benjamite” (Psa 7, title), and in its plural form, Shigionoth, it heads the prayer of Habakkuk the prophet (Hab 3:1). The word is most received as naming a song of irregular and impassioned movement — a strain that surges and breaks like the heaving of a soul under assault, casting itself by turns into complaint, into pleading, into triumph. Such is the seventh psalm: it opens in alarm, “O LORD my God, in thee do I put my trust: save me from all them that persecute me” (Psa 7:1), pleads David’s integrity in the matter, calls upon the righteous Judge, and closes in settled praise, “I will praise the LORD according to his righteousness” (Psa 7:17). The prayer of Habakkuk runs the same course, from trembling to faith. Let the believer mark the comfort here: the Shiggaion teaches that even disordered grief, when it is poured out before God, becomes ordered worship. The soul need not compose itself before it comes; it may come reeling, and the LORD will steady it. The song that begins in a storm of feeling may end, by grace, in the calm of trust.
webster_summary: A wild, irregular, impassioned ode; a song of strong and varied emotion poured out before the LORD.
webster_full: SHIGGAION, a Hebrew term in the title of the seventh psalm, denoting an irregular or impassioned song.
It is referred to a root signifying to wander or to reel, as of a strain of varied and surging movement.
The plural form, Shigionoth, heads the prayer of Habakkuk the prophet.
It names a song that moves by turns through complaint, pleading, and triumph.
It witnesses that grief poured out before God is turned into ordered worship.
scriptures: Shiggaion of David, which he sang unto the LORD, concerning the words of Cush the Benjamite.
O LORD my God, in thee do I put my trust: save me from all them that persecute me, and deliver me:
A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet upon Shigionoth.
I will praise the LORD according to his righteousness: and will sing praise to the name of the LORD most high.
corruption_summary: A song-form of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it teaches that even reeling grief, brought to God, is sanctified into worship.
corruption_paragraphs: Shiggaion names a manner of holy song and faces no postmodern redefinition. The temptation it answers is as old as the heart: to suppose the soul must be calm and composed before it dares approach God, and so to stay away in the very hour of need, ashamed of its disorder.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD welcomes the reeling soul. David came concerning the slanders of Cush in a storm of feeling and left in settled praise; Habakkuk trembled and yet rejoiced in the God of his salvation (Hab 3:18). The saint may come as he is, pour out the wild strain, and trust the Spirit to compose it, by the psalm’s end, into the calm of faith.
roots_summary: From a Hebrew root meaning to wander or reel, Shiggaion names an irregular, impassioned song that ends, by grace, in settled trust.
roots_lines: Shiggaion — Hebrew shiggāyōn, perhaps from shāgāh, to reel or wander.

Such songs move from complaint and pleading to settled praise.
usage: The Shiggaion teaches that disordered grief, poured out before God, becomes ordered worship.
The soul need not compose itself before it comes; it may come reeling, and the LORD will steady it.
Like David and Habakkuk, the saint may begin in a storm of feeling and end in the calm of trust.

etymology: Hebrew neginōth, plural of negināh, from nāgan, “to touch the strings, to play a stringed instrument”; music made upon strings, as harp, psaltery, and lyre.
biblical_def: Neginoth is the direction “to the chief Musician on Neginoth,” standing over several psalms (4, 6, 54, 55, 67, 76) and answered in Habakkuk’s closing word, “to the chief singer on my stringed instruments” (Hab 3:19). It appoints the psalm to be sung with the accompaniment of strings. The worship of Israel was no formless thing left to the whim of the worshipper; David, by the word of the LORD through Gad and Nathan, set the Levites in their courses “to be the singers with instruments of musick, psalteries and harps and cymbals” (1Ch 15:16; 2Ch 29:25). Neginoth witnesses to that ordered, appointed praise. The strings were no mere ornament but the servants of the word, lifting the holy text upon a fitting tune that the congregation might sing it together with one heart and voice. Let the believer learn the principle that abides through every age: God is to be worshipped not as men devise, but as He appoints; with reverence and order, “decently and in order” (1Co 14:40), the affections engaged and the body bowed, the whole man and the whole assembly brought under the rule of His revealed will. The form serves the word, and the word serves the glory of God.
webster_summary: Stringed instruments, or music upon strings; the direction appointing a psalm to be sung with such accompaniment.
webster_full: NEGINOTH, a Hebrew word in the titles of several psalms, signifying stringed instruments.
It is derived from a root meaning to touch the strings or to play upon them.
The direction “to the chief Musician on Neginoth” appoints the psalm to be sung with strings.
It witnesses to the ordered, appointed worship David set among the Levites.
It teaches that the form of worship is the servant of the word and the glory of God.
scriptures: To the chief Musician on Neginoth, A Psalm of David.
The LORD God is my strength, and he will make my feet like hinds’ feet, and he will make me to walk upon mine high places. To the chief singer on my stringed instruments.
And David spake to the chief of the Levites to appoint their brethren to be the singers with instruments of musick, psalteries and harps and cymbals, sounding, by lifting up the voice with joy.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
corruption_summary: A direction for ordered praise; it rebukes the modern drift from reverent, appointed worship toward performance staged for the worshipper’s entertainment.
corruption_paragraphs: Neginoth itself faces no postmodern redefinition, but the worship it served is everywhere under pressure. The age tends to treat the gathering of the saints as a concert — a stage, a spectacle, a performance measured by its power to move and to please the crowd — rather than as the appointed, reverent, congregational praise of a holy God who has told us how He will be worshipped.

The principle to recover is order under the word. The strings of Neginoth were appointed servants of the holy text, set in their place by David at God’s direction, that the whole congregation might sing as one. Worship is not ours to devise after the fashion of the world; it is to be rendered “decently and in order,” the form forever bowing to the word it carries and to the glory of the God it adores.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for playing upon strings, Neginoth appoints a psalm to ordered, instrument-bearing congregational praise.
roots_lines: Neginoth — Hebrew neginōth, from nāgan, to play upon strings.

Habakkuk closes “to the chief singer on my stringed instruments.”
David appointed the Levites with psalteries, harps, and cymbals (1Ch 15:16).
It witnesses to ordered worship, the form serving the word.
usage: Neginoth marks the appointed, reverent praise of Israel, the strings made servants of the holy word.
God is worshipped not as men devise but as He appoints, decently and in order.
The form of worship forever bows to the word it carries and the glory of the God it adores.

etymology: Hebrew nechīlōth, of uncertain root; by the most received account from chālīl, “a pipe, a flute” (the bored or perforated reed), thus wind instruments; the King James margin reads “flutes.”
biblical_def: Nehiloth appears but once in all the Scriptures, in the title of the fifth psalm: “To the chief Musician upon Nehiloth, A Psalm of David” (Psa 5, title). The word is obscure, yet most have understood it of wind instruments — the pipe or flute, the breath-driven reed — as the King James translators noted in their margin. The psalm it heads is David’s morning prayer: “My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up” (Psa 5:3). If Nehiloth indeed names the flute, then the whole instrument of man is here brought to the worship of God — the strings of Neginoth and the breath of Nehiloth alike, that nothing in the worshipper be withheld. The psalmist bids the saints praise the LORD “with stringed instruments and organs” (Psa 150:4), the breath of life returned in song to Him who gave it. Let the believer take warning too from the very obscurity of the term: there are things in the inspired text we cannot now fully expound, and humility, not invention, becomes us there. What is plain is enough — that David rose early to seek his God, and would have his every faculty, breath and voice and instrument, consecrated to that holy end.
webster_summary: Wind instruments, or flutes; the obscure direction over David’s morning prayer in the fifth psalm.
webster_full: NEHILOTH, a Hebrew word found only in the title of the fifth psalm.
It is most received as denoting wind instruments, the pipe or flute, and the margin reads “flutes.”
It heads David’s morning prayer, in which he directs his prayer unto the LORD and looks up.
If it names the flute, it brings the breath of man, with the strings, into the worship of God.
Its very obscurity teaches humility before what the inspired text does not fully unfold.
scriptures: To the chief Musician upon Nehiloth, A Psalm of David.
My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up.
Praise him with the timbrel and dance: praise him with stringed instruments and organs.
But as for me, I will come into thy house in the multitude of thy mercy: and in thy fear will I worship toward thy holy temple.
corruption_summary: An obscure worship-direction, not a contested doctrine; it teaches humility before what the inspired text does not unfold, and the consecration of every faculty to God.
corruption_paragraphs: Nehiloth faces no postmodern redefinition. The lesson of its obscurity cuts rather against a perennial fault of the proud heart — the refusal to let any word stand unmastered, the itch to invent a certainty where the LORD has left a holy reticence. The word means, most likely, the flute; beyond that the godly are content not to press.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is twofold: humility before the text, and the consecration of the whole man to worship. David rose in the morning and looked up; he would have voice and breath and instrument alike laid upon the altar of praise. The saint gives God not a part but the whole — every faculty, every early hour, every breath that He first gave.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew most likely meaning flutes, Nehiloth heads David’s morning prayer and teaches the consecration of every faculty to God.

It is found only in the title of the fifth psalm.
The King James margin renders it “flutes.”

Its obscurity teaches humility before what the text does not fully unfold.
usage: If Nehiloth names the flute, then breath as well as string is consecrated to the worship of God.
The obscurity of the word teaches humility: where Scripture is reticent, invention does not become us.
David rose in the morning and looked up, his every faculty laid upon the altar of praise.

etymology: Hebrew shemīnīth, “the eighth,” from shemōneh, “eight”; understood as the octave below, the lower or bass register, or an eight-stringed instrument; set over against Alamoth, the higher voices.
biblical_def: Sheminith, “the eighth,” heads the sixth and the twelfth psalms, and is named in the order of David’s singers, where certain Levites played “with harps on the Sheminith to excel” (1Ch 15:21). It is most received as denoting the lower register — the octave beneath, the grave bass of the men’s voices and the deeper strings — set in deliberate contrast to Alamoth, the maidens’ or higher part (1Ch 15:20). The sixth psalm, sung upon Sheminith, is the first of the seven penitential psalms: “O LORD, rebuke me not in thine anger, neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure” (Psa 6:1), and the deep notes well befit so grave a cry. The twelfth likewise mourns the failing of the faithful from among men. Here is a quiet wisdom: the very registers of the congregation’s song were ordered under God, the high and the low, the maiden and the man, each given a part, that the whole assembly might lift a full and tempered praise. The body of Christ is no monotone. As in the temple choir the deep voices answered the high, so in the church the strong and the weak, the glad and the grieving, blend their distinct notes into one harmony before the throne.
webster_summary: The eighth, or the lower octave; the bass register of the temple song, set over against the higher Alamoth.
webster_full: SHEMINITH, a Hebrew word signifying “the eighth,” from the number eight.
It is most received as denoting the octave below, the bass or lower register of voices and strings.
It heads the sixth and twelfth psalms and is named in the order of David’s singers.
It is set in contrast to Alamoth, the higher or maidens’ part.
It witnesses that the very registers of the congregation’s praise were ordered under God.
scriptures: To the chief Musician on Neginoth upon Sheminith, A Psalm of David.
To the chief Musician upon Sheminith, A Psalm of David.
And Mattithiah, and Elipheleh, and Mikneiah, and Obededom, and Jeiel, and Azaziah, with harps on the Sheminith to excel.
O LORD, rebuke me not in thine anger, neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure.
corruption_summary: A direction of register, not a contested doctrine; it pictures the ordered harmony of the whole congregation, the deep voices answering the high before the throne.
corruption_paragraphs: Sheminith names the lower register of the temple song and faces no postmodern redefinition. The truth it pictures, however, stands against both a flattening uniformity and a chaos of self-expression in worship: the body of Christ is neither a monotone nor a babel, but a tempered harmony in which every appointed part has its place.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ordered fulness of congregational praise. As the deep voices upon Sheminith answered the high voices upon Alamoth, so in the church the strong and the weak, the rejoicing and the penitent, lift their distinct notes into one harmony. None is left out, and none is left to himself; all are gathered under the rule of the word into a single song to God.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “the eighth,” Sheminith names the lower octave of the temple song, the deep voices answering the high in ordered praise.

It denotes the octave below, the bass or lower register.

It is set over against Alamoth, the higher or maidens’ part.
usage: The deep notes of Sheminith befit the penitential cry of the sixth psalm.

The body of Christ is no monotone: strong and weak, glad and grieving, blend into one harmony.

etymology: Hebrew gittīth, from Gath; either an instrument or tune of Gath, where David sojourned, or a melody “of the winepresses,” since gath signifies a winepress; borne by three psalms of holy gladness.
biblical_def: Gittith heads three psalms, and all three are songs of holy gladness: the eighth, which exults in the glory of the LORD’s name through all creation; the eighty-first, the feast-day summons to obey and rejoice; and the eighty-fourth, the pilgrim’s longing for the courts of God. The word looks back to Gath. If it names an instrument or air David learned in that Philistine city of his wanderings, then it tells of an exile’s sorrow turned to a saint’s song. If it means “of the winepress,” from gath, then it joins these psalms to the joy of harvest and ingathering, when the treaders shout for the new wine. Either reading breathes the same gladness. The eighth opens, “O LORD our Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth!” (Psa 8:1); the eighty-fourth, “How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts!” (Psa 84:1). Let the believer mark that the LORD appoints His people not only psalms of penitence but psalms of pure joy, and that the joy of the LORD is their strength (Neh 8:10). The grapes are trodden that the wine may gladden the heart; the saint is pressed by providence that praise may flow. Gittith is a vintage-song of the redeemed.
webster_summary: An instrument or tune of Gath, or a melody of the winepresses; the glad key of three psalms of joy and longing.
webster_full: GITTITH, a Hebrew word in the titles of the eighth, eighty-first, and eighty-fourth psalms.
It is referred to Gath, either as an instrument or tune of that city, or as a melody of the winepresses.
All three psalms it heads are songs of holy gladness, glory, and longing for the courts of God.
If “of the winepress,” it joins them to the joy of harvest and ingathering.
It witnesses that the LORD appoints His people psalms of pure joy as well as of penitence.
scriptures: To the chief Musician upon Gittith, A Psalm of David.
O LORD our Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth! who hast set thy glory above the heavens.
To the chief Musician upon Gittith, A Psalm for the sons of Korah.
How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts!
corruption_summary: A glad worship-direction, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the place of pure joy in worship, the vintage-song of a redeemed and rejoicing people.
corruption_paragraphs: Gittith faces no postmodern redefinition. The truth it carries answers a heaviness that can settle on sober religion: the notion that reverence must always be grave, and that gladness is a lighter, lesser thing unbefitting the worship of God. The three Gittith psalms rebuke that gloom; they are reverent and exultant at once.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the holy gladness of true worship. The same God who gave the penitential psalms gave the vintage-songs, for the joy of the LORD is the strength of His people. If the word means “of the winepress,” it preaches a sweet providence: the grapes are trodden that the wine may gladden, and the saint is pressed by trials that praise may flow the richer.
roots_summary: From Gath, an instrument or a winepress-melody, Gittith heads three psalms of holy gladness, glory, and longing for the courts of God.

Either an instrument or tune of Gath, the city of David’s sojourn.
Or a melody “of the winepresses,” from gath, a winepress.
It heads the eighth, eighty-first, and eighty-fourth psalms.
All three are songs of holy gladness, glory, and longing.
usage: Gittith is a vintage-song of the redeemed: the grapes are trodden that the wine may gladden the heart.
The LORD appoints His people psalms of pure joy as well as of penitence.
Reverence and gladness meet in the Gittith psalms: How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts.

etymology: Hebrew mūth labbēn, “the death of the son” or “to die for the son” (mūth, death; labbēn, for or to the son); an obscure title or tune-name found only at the ninth psalm.
biblical_def: Muth-labben stands over the ninth psalm alone: “To the chief Musician upon Muthlabben, A Psalm of David” (Psa 9, title). The words, taken as Hebrew, signify “the death of the son,” and many of the godly, reading them so, have heard a foregleam of the death of the Son of God. Others take Muthlabben as the name of a tune now lost to us, or as a corruption of some occasion in David’s life. Whatever the title’s first intent, the psalm beneath it is a song of triumphant praise to the LORD as the righteous Judge of all the earth: “I will praise thee, O LORD, with my whole heart; I will shew forth all thy marvellous works” (Psa 9:1). It rises to the great assurance, “he shall judge the world in righteousness, he shall minister judgment to the people in uprightness” (Psa 9:8), and comforts the afflicted, “The LORD also will be a refuge for the oppressed, a refuge in times of trouble” (Psa 9:9). The believer cannot read “the death of the son” without thinking upon Him who died and rose, and who shall judge the quick and the dead. So even this dark and disputed title is lit from the cross: the death of the Son is the ground of the righteous judgment, and the refuge of all the oppressed who flee to Him.
webster_summary: “The death of the son”; an obscure title over the ninth psalm, in which the godly have heard a foregleam of the death of God’s Son.
webster_full: MUTH-LABBEN, a Hebrew title found only over the ninth psalm.
Taken as Hebrew, the words signify “the death of the son” or “to die for the son.”
Many of the godly have heard in it a foregleam of the death of the Son of God.
Others take it as the name of a tune now lost, or an occasion in David’s life.
The psalm beneath it is a song of triumph in the LORD as the righteous Judge.
scriptures: To the chief Musician upon Muthlabben, A Psalm of David.
I will praise thee, O LORD, with my whole heart; I will shew forth all thy marvellous works.
And he shall judge the world in righteousness, he shall minister judgment to the people in uprightness.

corruption_summary: A disputed title lit from the cross; the entry faces no postmodern redefinition, but the apostolic habit of finding Christ in every dark line of the Psalter must be recovered against a flattening literalism.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live error is rather a method: the refusal to read the Psalter Christianly, treating every shadow and obscure title as a mere antiquarian puzzle, and forbidding the believer to hear in “the death of the son” any whisper of the Son who died. By that rule the Psalms are emptied of the very Christ the apostles found everywhere in them.

The principle to recover is that Christ is the substance and key of the Psalter. Our Lord Himself opened the disciples’ understanding to the things written of Him “in the psalms” (Luk 24:44). The saint reads the ninth psalm as the song of a righteous Judge whose judgment seat is founded on the death of His own Son; the dark title becomes a doorway to the cross, and the refuge of the oppressed is the crucified and risen King.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “the death of the son,” Muth-labben heads a psalm of triumph in the righteous Judge, read by the godly as a foregleam of the cross.
roots_lines: Muth-labben — Hebrew mūth labbēn, “the death of the son.”
It is found only over the ninth psalm.
Many of the godly hear in it a foregleam of the death of God’s Son.
Others take it as a lost tune-name or an occasion in David’s life.
The psalm beneath is a song of triumph in the LORD the righteous Judge.
usage: Even the dark title Muth-labben is lit from the cross: the death of the Son grounds the righteous judgment.
Christ opened the understanding to the things written of Him in the psalms (Luk 24:44).
The refuge of the oppressed in the ninth psalm is the crucified and risen King.

etymology: Hebrew ayyeleth ha-shachar, “the hind of the morning” or “the deer of the dawn” (ayyeleth, a hind; shachar, dawn, morning); the tune or theme set over the twenty-second psalm, the great psalm of the cross.
biblical_def: Aijeleth Shahar, “the hind of the morning,” stands over the twenty-second psalm (Psa 22, title), the most piercing of all the messianic psalms. Whether it names an old melody to which the psalm was set, or a figure of its theme, the image is fitting beyond measure: the gentle hind run down by its hunters at break of day is the suffering Saviour, hunted to death in the dark night of the cross and rising in the morning of resurrection. For this psalm opens with the very cry our Lord uttered upon the tree: “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Psa 22:1), which Matthew records from His own lips (Mat 27:46). It foretells, a thousand years before Calvary, the mocking of the bystanders, the piercing of His hands and His feet, and the parting of His garments by lot: “they pierced my hands and my feet” (Psa 22:16). David never suffered these things; the Spirit spoke through him of Great David’s greater Son. And the psalm that begins in forsaking ends in a worldwide kingdom: “all the ends of the world shall remember and turn unto the LORD” (Psa 22:27). The hind of the morning is hunted at dusk that a multitude no man can number may rejoice at dawn.
webster_summary: “The hind of the morning”; the title over the twenty-second psalm, picturing the hunted, suffering, and risen Christ.
webster_full: AIJELETH SHAHAR, a Hebrew phrase signifying “the hind of the morning” or “the deer of the dawn.”
It stands over the twenty-second psalm, the great psalm of the crucifixion.
Whether a tune-name or a figure of the theme, it pictures the gentle hind hunted at daybreak.
The image befits the suffering Christ, run down to death and rising in the morning.
The psalm foretells the cross a thousand years before it came to pass.
scriptures: To the chief Musician upon Aijeleth Shahar, A Psalm of David.
My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?
For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet.
And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
corruption_summary: The crucifixion psalm; the entry faces no postmodern redefinition, but the critical denial that Psalm 22 is true prophecy of Christ must be answered from the Gospels themselves.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error to name is the modern critical insistence that the twenty-second psalm describes only David’s own distress, the pierced hands and parted garments dismissed as poetic exaggeration or read away by altering the text. By that account the most exact prophecy of the cross in all the Old Testament becomes a coincidence, and the agreement with Calvary an accident.

The principle to recover is that the Spirit who inspired the psalm fulfilled it to the letter. Our Lord took its opening cry upon His own lips; the evangelists record the mocking, the lots cast for His vesture, and the piercing, in the very words of David’s song. David did not have his hands and feet pierced; the hind of the morning is Christ, and the psalm is His. To read it otherwise is to be ashamed of the plainest prophecy of the cross.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “the hind of the morning,” Aijeleth Shahar titles the twenty-second psalm, the prophecy of the hunted, crucified, and risen Christ.
roots_lines: Aijeleth Shahar — Hebrew ayyeleth ha-shachar, “the hind of the morning.”
It stands over the twenty-second psalm, the great psalm of the cross.
The hind hunted at dawn pictures the suffering and rising Saviour.
The psalm opens with the cry Christ uttered upon the tree (Mat 27:46).
It foretells the piercing of His hands and feet (Psa 22:16).
usage: The hind of the morning is hunted at dusk that a multitude may rejoice at dawn.
David never suffered the piercing of Psalm 22; the Spirit spoke through him of David’s greater Son.
The psalm that begins in forsaking ends in a worldwide kingdom turning unto the LORD.

etymology: Hebrew machālath, perhaps from chālāh, “to be sick, weak, or grieved,” thus a sorrowful strain; or the name of a mournful tune; found at the fifty-third and (as Mahalath Leannoth) the eighty-eighth psalm.
biblical_def: Mahalath heads two psalms of heaviness. The fifty-third, “upon Mahalath,” is the lament over the corruption of the whole race of man: “The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God” (Psa 53:1). The eighty-eighth, “upon Mahalath Leannoth” — to be sung concerning affliction, or “to afflict” — is the darkest psalm in all the Psalter, the cry of Heman the Ezrahite from the very brink of the pit: “LORD, why castest thou off my soul? why hidest thou thy face from me?” (Psa 88:14). If the word indeed bespeaks sickness or grief, it is the fit key for songs sung out of the depths, when the soul is faint and the comforts of God seem far. Here is a tender provision of the LORD: He gives His people not only triumph-songs but grief-songs, and sets them in the inspired hymnbook of the church. The eighty-eighth ends in darkness, with no sunrise in its final line — and yet it is a prayer, addressed all through to “O LORD God of my salvation” (Psa 88:1). So Mahalath teaches that faith may grope in the dark and still hold fast; that the believer overwhelmed may yet pray; and that even the song which finds no light before its end is heard, and treasured, and answered in God’s own time.
webster_summary: A mournful strain or tune, bespeaking sickness or grief; the key of the fifty-third psalm and the dark eighty-eighth.
webster_full: MAHALATH, a Hebrew word in the titles of the fifty-third and eighty-eighth psalms.
It is referred to a root signifying sickness, weakness, or grief, and may name a mournful tune.
The eighty-eighth adds Leannoth, “to afflict,” and is the darkest psalm in the Psalter.
It heads the cry of Heman the Ezrahite from the very brink of the pit.
It witnesses that the LORD gives His people grief-songs as well as triumph-songs.
scriptures: To the chief Musician upon Mahalath, Maschil, A Psalm of David.
A Song or Psalm for the sons of Korah, to the chief Musician upon Mahalath Leannoth, Maschil of Heman the Ezrahite.
LORD, why castest thou off my soul? why hidest thou thy face from me?
The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. Corrupt are they, and have done abominable iniquity: there is none that doeth good.
corruption_summary: A grief-song of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it answers the modern shame of lament with the LORD’s own provision of psalms for the darkest hours.
corruption_paragraphs: Mahalath faces no postmodern redefinition. The fault it answers belongs to a religion of relentless cheerfulness, which mistakes the silencing of sorrow for the conquest of it, and leaves the grieving saint no words but a forced smile. The Psalter knows better; it sets the eighty-eighth psalm, which ends in darkness, into the very songbook of the worshipping church.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sanctity of lament. Heman’s psalm gropes in the dark and finds no sunrise before its final line, yet it is a prayer throughout, addressed to the God of his salvation. Mahalath teaches that faith may be overwhelmed and still pray; that the believer need not pretend; and that the song which finds no light before its end is still heard, treasured, and answered in God’s appointed time.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for sickness or grief, Mahalath names a mournful strain, the key of the dark eighty-eighth psalm of Heman the Ezrahite.
roots_lines: Mahalath — Hebrew machālath, perhaps from chālāh, to be sick or grieved.
It heads the fifty-third psalm, the lament over the corruption of man.
As Mahalath Leannoth it heads the eighty-eighth, the darkest of all the psalms.
That psalm is the cry of Heman the Ezrahite from the brink of the pit.
It witnesses that the LORD gives His people grief-songs as well as triumph-songs.
usage: Mahalath teaches that faith may grope in the dark and still hold fast to the God of its salvation.
The eighty-eighth psalm ends in darkness, yet it is a prayer throughout: the believer need not pretend.
The LORD sets grief-songs in the inspired hymnbook, that the overwhelmed saint may yet pray.
